doc.title: Ralph Sutton interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 22, 1995

title: Singers he accompanied, including Lee Wiley
summary: He names Rushing, Maxine Sullivan and Teagarden and tells of tempo trouble with Lee Wiley at the Vanguard.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them

blocks.x: Who are some of the singers that you’ve played behind that you enjoyed.

Jimmy Rushing. He was one of my favorites. Well Jack Teagarden sang. I remember working at the Village Vanguard behind Maxine Sullivan, who I adored. And there’s another girl singer, Chippy Hill, yeah. But Lee Wiley, I remember I played behind her at the Village Vanguard with Max Kaminsky and Arthur Trappier, he took Slick Jones’ place on drums with Fats Waller. We were working as a trio at the Vanguard and Lee Wiley was married to Jess Stacey at the time. And she came in, she was on the show at the Village Vanguard. And I don’t whether she and Jess were getting along too well or not, but you could never get that tempo right for Lee Wiley you know? We’d have a rehearsal and she’d want to sing at this tempo, and I’d try to set the tempo I remember like she liked to sing it. And she’d turn around you know and give you a look, and I’m

thinking, I’m going to stay away from singers, man. But anyway, I loved Lee singing you know. I’ll never forget her coming into Eddie Condon’s club later on. I can’t say what our conversation was about, I mean we were very friendly. But she sort of apologized to me for being very sarcastic sometimes on the job you know. But we settled it. There was no problem.
Yeah, working with singers can be a little nerve wracking occasionally. Especially if you hit a chord they don’t particularly like and it throws them off, and you get one of those looks.

I always thought for the most part that you couldn’t compare singers with musicians, you know what I mean? You work with a wonderful guy like Jimmy Rushing or Jack Teagarden or somebody singing, there was no problems at all, it was right in there you know. But it didn’t always work you know.
Yeah. I think it probably helps when a singer is a player of an instrument.
Yeah, and knows what’s going on.
They are able to hear and deal with little things that come up a little more gracefully. When a singer stops, that’s when you start going ohhh—
